t: Handling Sum Queries After Update — Segment Tree with Flip Laziness
o: nums1 is binary; type 1 flips a range of nums1, type 2 adds p * nums1[i] to every nums2[i], type 3 asks for sum(nums2). The key realization: a type-2 query changes sum(nums2) by exactly p * (number of ones currently in nums1), and type 3 just reports the maintained total — we never need to touch nums2 itself. So the only hard part is a data structure over nums1 supporting range flip and global count of ones. Example 1: after flipping index 1, nums1 has three ones, so type 2 adds 3 and type 3 answers 3. With n, q up to 1e5, brute force is O(nq) = 1e10 — too slow; a segment tree with lazy flip gives O(log n) per query.
k: Type 2 and type 3 only need the count of ones in nums1, not nums2 itself — maintain a single scalar total.
A segment tree storing the count of ones per node supports range flip in O(log n) via lazy reversal: flipped node count = length - count.

a.i: Directly flip ranges and recompute sums per query. Correct but O(n) per type-1/type-2 query, which times out at 1e5 scale; useful to establish semantics.
s: Copy nums1, compute total of nums2.
Type 1: flip each index in the range. Type 2: total += p * sum(nums1). Type 3: append total.
a.t: O(n·q) — each type-1 or type-2 query scans the array

a.n: Approach 2: Lazy segment tree over nums1
a.i: Each node stores the count of ones in its range plus a pending-flip flag. Flipping a fully covered node replaces its count with length − count and toggles the flag; pushes happen only when descending. Type 2 adds p * root-count to the running total; type 3 reads it.
s: Build the tree from nums1 with counts.
Type 2: total += p * cnt[root]. Type 3: append total.
a.t: O((n + q) log n) — building is O(n), each type-1 query touches O(log n) nodes; types 2/3 are O(1)
a.sp: O(n) — segment tree arrays of size 4n

w: Always state the reduction to 'count of ones' first — it collapses types 2 and 3 to scalar bookkeeping. Pitfalls: forgetting to push lazy flags before recursing, 32-bit overflow of the total (use 64-bit), and off-by-one on inclusive ranges. Follow-ups: support range-add on nums2 with a second lazy tree, or answer type-3 as sum over a subrange.
